newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler to make 180,000 flexible-fuel vans.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler to make 180,000 flexible-fuel vans.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said on Tuesday it would build about 180,000 minivans with engines capable of running on either gasoline or a mix of ethanol and gasoline.
The vehicles will be available starting in the 1998 model year, which begins this autumn, Chrysler officials said at the Governors' Ethanol Coalition Conference here.
Ford Motor Co. said last week it plans to produce 250,000 flexible-fuel pickup trucks, sedans and minivans starting in the autumn of 1998 for the 1999 model year.
Ford said it will spend about $300 to convert the vehicles' engines so they can run on both gasoline and a mixture of gasoline and ethanol.
Ethanol, made from corn and other grains, burns cleaner than gasoline but is less fuel-efficient.
A Chrysler official would not comment on how much it will cost the automaker to adapt the flexible-fuel technology, but he said it will not affect the retail price of the minivans.

Chrysler said flexible-fuel minivans that run on E85 -- a combination of 85 percent ethanol and 15 percent gasoline -- will get about 33 percent fewer miles per gallon than minivans that run on gasoline.
All of Chrysler's 1998 Plymouth Voyager, Dodge Caravan and Chrysler Town and Country minivans that come with the standard 3.3-liter, six-cylinder engine will have flexible-fuel capability.
In addition to helping the enivronment, Chrysler officials said flexible-fuel vehicles help lower U.S. dependence on oil imports.
"Chrysler recognizes the importance and potential of using alternative fuels, and especially of ethanol," said Mike Clement, Chrysler's manager of alternative-fuel vehicle sales and marketing.

Chrysler officials said little about the federal fuel credits automakers receive for offering flexible-fuel vehicles. Such credits allow automakers to raise their corporate average fuel economy, or CAFE. That, in turn, allows them to sell more of the highly profitable -- but less fuel-efficient -- pickup trucks and sport/utility vehicles.
The federal government sets CAFE limits to force automakers to offer a certain number of fuel-efficient vehicles.
